toc.title: What noise does to your body
Building up to silence, step by step
Simple ways to add silence to your day

blocks.p: You want to be more mindful to reduce negative emotions like stress, anxiety, worry, and panic. But finding time for long meditative sessions can be a challenge, and silence is too difficult. What if there's an easier way to bring mindfulness into your day?

Here's a simple, but I think essential, mindfulness ingredient: small moments of silence in your daily routine. Doing so helps you practice feeling safe and reduce your negative emotional experiences.

I think silence is pretty essential for mindfulness. Yes, you can do mindfulness with sound, and I'll come back to that. But if you can exist in more quiet or more silence than not, I think it can be really powerful.

We're constantly surrounded by noise and stimulation. Silence gives us more of a chance to pause, to breathe, and to simply be. In these quieter moments, I think we're more likely to tune into our bodies and our surroundings, and to practice mindfulness closer to its purest form.

I would argue that the natural condition of life is silence, especially before technology and cities. Silence must have been constant. It must have been ever present. There were always sounds, of course: neighbors, animals, trees in the wind. But underneath that was a constant and steady stream of accessible silence.

The way I think about it, silence was a friend. When noise disrupted the silence, our bodies neurocepted that sound as safety or danger. We heard it through our ears, which sent a signal to the brainstem, which detected safety, danger, or life threat. The stereotypical crack of a twig being stepped on by a predator alerts us to possible danger. Or the low rumble of an avalanche in the distance, or the squawking of birds that means a predator is near. So in my mind, silence, and the breaking of silence, went hand in hand with survival. And being able to be at peace in silence is what led those before us to survive.
I think that's a big struggle for many people now. We don't access that level of true, natural silence day to day. I don't think we even have a good concept of it.

Check your level of silence right now. Just listen. What do you hear? Maybe it's quiet where you are, but I doubt there's actual silence. You'll likely hear people in the background, traffic in the distance, the hum of a fluorescent light above you, the hum of a refrigerator. Silence still exists, but we're effectively cut off from it pretty much constantly. In place of the stillness that would come with friendly silence, we're left with the unease that comes from the unrelenting noise we're immersed in.

I once did a guided cave exploration. We went pretty deep underground, and we were able to access a level of silence I just don't have a reference point for outside of that cave. They also did an experiment where they turned off every single light, all the phones, the watches, everything, and there was pure and complete darkness. I can make a room dark, but it's never so perfectly dark that you actually lose your sense of sight. Same thing with sound. It was silent, and anything that made a noise, you'd pick up on.

That's not something we experience anymore. In large part, the real, actual danger around us has been eliminated, depending on where you live. Of course there's still danger, but for the most part we can put our earbuds in and walk around wherever we want without worrying about a tiger pouncing on us and eating us. So that's nice. But we've also lost touch with natural silence.

blocks.h: What noise does to your body

blocks.p: So you might not be aware of it, but your body is probably in some constant low level of sympathetic activation. The sympathetic system is responsible for your ability to mobilize. You use mobilization when you're playing or dancing, but you also use it for running and fighting when you're in danger.

Being in a sympathetic state doesn't mean you're actually running away or fighting right now. But you probably have some constant low level of mobilization in your body, and you'll notice it because it feels like stress, anxiety, anger, overwhelm, or more.

Noise can trigger this sympathetic state. The last time someone scared you, you probably tensed up. Part of that tensing up is the mobilization system kicking on. But it also kind of gets locked in place, because the immobilization system kicks on as well.

Think about listening to music. If you have music on, there's a good chance you're tapping your foot, or maybe you're full-on dancing. The sound of the music is mobilizing you. Constant background noise has the same impact. It might not make you dance, but it mobilizes you, maybe slightly. You might not even notice it. But if you paused and listened inwardly, you might notice some tension, anxiousness, or unease.

Here's an experiment you could try. Go into a space like your kitchen or bathroom and turn on the fan, like the hood fan over the stove. Leave it on and hang out in that area for a while. Eventually you get used to it, and you don't really recognize it anymore, but it's still there in the background affecting your body. After a set amount of time you decide, maybe an hour or a couple of hours, turn it off and see how you feel.

I notice this in my own life. After we're done cooking and I turn off the hood fan, I notice that I'm activated. When the sound goes away, I become very aware of that activation. I feel it in my chest as a kind of pressure or tightness, and emotionally it feels like irritation.

Let's connect this to mindfulness. Mindfulness is the ability to connect with, and attune to, the present moment. It leads to connection with the external environment, and with your internal environment: your internal world, your body. So mindfulness and connection go together.

But to get to mindfulness and connection, you have to have actual, literal, external safety: a safe environment. From that safe environment, you have a chance to exist in your body's neurophysiological state of safety, its ventral vagal pathways. These are responsible for your ability to connect and socially engage, and also to be in the present moment, and to be in stillness: to be immobile and be okay with it.

If you're constantly mobilized in a defensive state, even a little bit, you never quite get to a true felt sense of safety and connection. It's still possible, of course. But if you're stuck in a defensive state, and the background noise is adding to it, getting to safety and into mindfulness is more challenging. So I would argue that the unrelenting noise around us decreases our ability to be in our safety state.

One obvious solution is to simply decrease the noise around you. Some things you can control: phone speakers, the TV, the computer, the stereo in the house or car. Some things you can't, like traffic in the distance. You could unplug your fridge, but I don't recommend it. The point is, if you can reduce the sound around you, you can get closer to reconnecting with your natural friend, silence.

I'm sure you're saying, "Yeah, but I don't like silence. That's when I feel more activated." That might be your reality. Silence can be uncomfortable for many people, and especially if you're stuck in a traumatized state, it can feel very unsafe. If you're in a flight or fight state, or a freeze state, you might prefer noise. You might prefer something to focus on, to remind yourself that you're actually safe: "If I can hear the TV or the white noise, there's no danger out there."

So you might listen to white noise or music, have the TV on, or use ASMR. These can be great, and I'm not telling you to stop. They can totally reduce your defensive activation. But they don't solve the problem. They're aids, not solutions. Keep using them if they're working for you.

The problem isn't the silence. The problem is the defensive state activation. Silence forces someone with chronic flight, fight, or freeze energy in their system to feel that autonomic dysregulation, and they feel it as emotions like anxiety, stress, or overwhelm. The sound reassures them. Silence might be too much.
Deb Dana named how tricky this is when she was on the podcast:

q: Stillness is the most complicated autonomic blend of states, because how do you come into quiet, into stillness, without stimulating shut down? It's a tricky thing to do, especially for people with a trauma history. Because stillness is a very vulnerable place and I have to really feel safe to come into stillness.
blocks.cite: Deb Dana, [Deb Dana Interview: Story Follows State, Climbing the Ladder and Diagnosing (episode 29)](https://player.captivate.fm/episode/f8b9643c-28f8-4185-9525-8b4e6301516c)

blocks.p: So the problem is being stuck in a defensive state, and the goal is to lower the defensive state activation. The solution, then, is to increase safety state activation. And the tool to do that is mindfulness.

When we practice mindfulness, we're not just being present. We're practicing being in our safety state, exercising those ventral vagal pathways. Over time, those pathways can get strong enough to tolerate higher levels of defensive activation, and they can definitely get strong enough to tolerate silence.

blocks.h: Building up to silence, step by step

blocks.p: Being mindful of defensive activation, like anxiety or fear, is probably too much to ask right now. So instead, I'd encourage you to be mindful of safety state activation when it's present, or to do things that bring it up. You'll know there's more safety in your system because you'll feel more connected to the present moment, to yourself, and to the environment around you. You'll breathe more easily into your belly, and you'll feel more relaxed.

ol: Be mindful with sound you find soothing. If you feel calmer with white noise, go right ahead. But experience it mindfully. Ask yourself, "What does this actually feel like for me, listening to this ASMR?"

Practice silent mindfulness in small moments. Once you can be mindful with a sound that brings up some safety, or reduces your defensive activation, the next step is silent mindfulness in small, tolerable doses. You might not do ten minutes at once. You might do thirty seconds.
Extend it a little at a time. If thirty seconds is tolerable, try it again later, or the next day, and extend it a bit further.

blocks.p: I don't need you on a cushion for an hour with your legs crossed and your eyes closed. Small moments throughout the day are amazing, and better than nothing at all. Be mindful of what it's like to fold laundry, wash your hands, or play with your kids. If you're out pulling weeds, ask yourself, "What does this feel like?" These are moments with some quiet, maybe not playing with your kids, that might be more tolerable for you.

Each of these comes with its own experience. You can feel the cold of the water on your hands as you wash them. You can feel your muscles tense as you pull a weed. Maybe you get a sense of satisfaction, like I do, when you fold the laundry just right. Maybe it's sipping your morning coffee, taking a short walk, or sitting quietly for a few minutes. Practice it, notice it, and build the strength of your safety state through these small moments of mindfulness. Then add more and more silence as you can.

blocks.why: This article talks about mindfulness. This practice gives you a few minutes of it.

blocks.h: Simple ways to add silence to your day

ul: Start your day with five minutes of silence before you reach for your phone.
Take short breaks throughout the day, even just a minute or two at work, to exist in silence.
Add movement. If you don't do well being still and silent, take a silent walk.
Eat a meal in silence. Focus on the taste and the texture, and take a breath between swallows.
Before bed, spend a few minutes in silence, and maybe use your imagination to anchor in safety.
Use noise canceling earbuds or headphones to dampen sound if you need to.

blocks.p: I personally love using silence in the morning. My summer routine has been to be the first one up. My family hasn't been waking up at 6:00 AM in the summer, so I've had many mornings alone in silence, and I like it a lot. Someone in my community called it rejuvenating when I shared it, and that's a really good word for it.

I just sit there and listen to what my body wants: drinking coffee or water, sitting outside on the deck or on the couch, reading, or just sitting and thinking in silence. I listen to what I need in that moment and follow the little impulses my body has to decide what to do. I still get ready for my day. I pack my lunch, get dressed, shower, all of that. I just do it in as much silence as I can. It's an hour to ninety minute routine, and I've been loving it.
